label: AQ 0030
title: The judge that could be pleased

questions.q: Isn't RL robust to noisy rewards?
questions.a: To random noise, largely: Gao et al.'s model says independent noise slows the gain without reversing it. Judge errors aren't random. AgentRewardBench found web-agent judges side with the agent's own reasoning and miss instruction details, and a policy can produce those on purpose.

teach.title: How it works: what the 15% turns into

questions.q: Would a better judge, or several, fix it?
questions.a: It helps without ending the problem. Coste et al. (ICLR 2024) found that cautious optimisation against an ensemble of reward models “practically eliminates overoptimization” when picking the best of many samples, and reduced it in RL. It is still a learned target, so I'd keep checking it against people.

teach.title: How it works: what the 15% turns into

questions.q: How would you notice the judge being gamed during training?
questions.a: My suggestions: have people label a fresh sample of the current policy's runs at intervals, and track judge–human agreement and the false-pass rate over time. If the reward climbs while human-checked success stays flat, stop or roll back.

teach.title: How it works: what the 15% turns into

questions.q: On what runs was Online-Mind2Web's 85.7% judge agreement measured, and why does that matter for an RL reward?
questions.a: On runs by six existing web agents, none trained against the judge. Once the judge is the reward, the policy's runs change to earn it, so agreement measured beforehand may no longer hold.

teach.title: How it works: what the 15% turns into

questions.q: A judge is wrong 15% of the time on both successes and failures. If the agent truly succeeds on 10% of 1,000 runs, what share of paid runs are real?
questions.a: About 39%: it pays 85 of the 100 successes and 135 of the 900 failures, and 85 ÷ 220 ≈ 0.39. At 50% success the same judge's share is 85%.

teach.title: How it works: what the 15% turns into

questions.q: What did AgentRewardBench find about model judges of web-agent runs?
questions.a: Across 12 judges and 1,302 runs, no judge reached 70% precision (share of passed runs that really succeeded), and judges easily agreed with the agent's reasoning even when it was wrong.
